metadata.title: Considerations for Complying with 21 CFR 211.110

candidates.statement: In general, FDA’s guidance documents do not establish legally enforceable responsibilities. 27 Instead, guidances describe the Agency’s current thinking on a topic and should be viewed only 28 as recommendations, unless specific regulatory or statutory requirements are cited. The use of 29 the word should in Agency guidances means that something is suggested or recommended, but 30 not required. 31
candidates.context: This guidance applies to the manufacture of human drug products, including biological products, 23 and animal drug products; these will be collectively referred to as drug products in this guidance. 24 This guidance does not apply to the manufacture of active ingredients. 25

candidates.statement: All manufacturers, regardless of whether they are using advanced manufacturing, should apply a 53 scientific- and risk-based approach to controlling processes and ensuring drug product quality. 54 This approach should be based on robust product and process understanding. Manufacturers 55 must maintain the process in a state of control over the life of the process to ensure drug product 56 quality, even as materials, equipment, production environment, personnel, and manufacturing 57 procedures change. 8 Planning and executing a system that monitors process performance and 58 drug product quality helps ensure that a state of control is maintained. An effective monitoring 59 system helps maintain a state of control in multiple ways, which include helping manufacturers: 60 (1) ensure that processes and controls are continuously capable of producing a drug product of 61 desired quality; and (2) identify areas for continual improvement. 9 In addition, § 211.110(a) 62 requires that manufacturers establish and follow written procedures “that describe the in-process 63 controls, and tests, or examinations to be conducted on appropriate samples of in-process 64 materials of each batch.” Section 211.110(c) also requires that in-process materials are “tested 65 for identity, strength, quality, and purity as appropriate, and approved or rejected by the quality 66
candidates.context: Advanced manufacturing is a term for an innovative pharmaceutical manufacturing technology 45 or approach that has the potential to improve the reliability and robustness of the manufacturing 46 process and supply chain and increase timely access to quality medicines for the American 47 public. Advanced manufacturing can integrate novel technological approaches, use established 48 techniques in an innovative way, or apply production methods in a new domain where there may 49 be limited experience or no defined best practices. Advanced manufacturing can potentially be 50 used for new or currently marketed large or small molecule drugs. 7 4 See 21 CFR parts 210 and 211.

candidates.statement: 6 Continuous manufacturing can be applied to some or all unit operations in a manufacturing process. This includes the approach in which active ingredient and drug product unit operations are integrated to form a single continuous manufacturing process. Manufacturers who use continuous manufacturing processes must still define batches to be tested for release under 21 CFR 211.165 and for other CGMP requirements, including the requirements in § 211.110 that ensure batch uniformity and drug product integrity. See also 21 CFR 210.3(b)(2) and the ICH guidance for industry Q13 Continuous Manufacturing of Drug Substances and Drug Products (March 2023).
candidates.context: 7 CDER established the Framework for Regulatory Advanced Manufacturing Evaluation (FRAME) initiative to prepare a regulatory framework to support the adoption of advanced manufacturing technologies that could bring benefits to patients. This guidance is being issued as part of the FRAME initiative. For more information on CDER’s FRAME initiative, see https://www.fda.gov/about-fda/center-drug-evaluation-and-research-cder/cders- framework-regulatory-advanced-manufacturing-evaluation-frame-initiative .

Manufacturers 106 should define the significant phases in their manufacturing processes; however, FDA evaluates 107 the adequacy of these determinations and the supporting scientific rationale during application 108 assessment and on inspection. The manufacturer should use a scientific- and risk-based approach 109 to determine what constitutes a significant phase and to justify when and where the appropriate 110 tests or examinations should occur relative to a significant phase. It is important to choose the 111 appropriate in-process controls, and tests, or examinations to ensure the quality of in-process 112 materials as well as the performance of the manufacturing process. Process monitoring and 113 control decisions that result in minor equipment and process adjustments do not typically need 114 additional quality unit 16 approval if all of the following conditions are met: (1) the adjustments 115 are within the preestablished and scientifically justified limits; (2) these limits have been 116 approved by the quality unit in the master production and control record and the control strategy; 117 and (3) the production data is reviewed by the quality unit before approval or rejection of a 118 batch. 17 , 18

candidates.statement: In addition to appropriate flexibility in where and when in-process sampling and testing should 130 occur, the regulations provide flexibility in how in-process material and drug product testing is 131 conducted. The preamble to the final rule states that a sampling plan “can mean both a plan for 132 collection of physical units for testing, or it can mean a schedule by which an examination of 133 some sort is done.” 20 Although in-process controls, and tests, or examinations of in-process 134 materials are required, 21 sampling does not necessarily require steps for physically removing in- 135 process materials to test their characteristics. Innovative technologies allow in-line, at-line, or 136 on-line measurements in place of physical sample removal for laboratory testing, 22 and these 137 measurements can be used in conjunction with process models. 138

candidates.statement: As described in Section III, § 211.110 provides flexibility in what in-process sampling and 161 testing should be done in addition to where, when, and how it should be done. Drug product 162 manufacturers must use appropriate in-process control, and testing, or examination strategies to 163 ensure that in-process materials can be meaningfully evaluated at significant phases. 24 This 164 evaluation allows the quality unit to make approval or rejection determinations for in-process 165 materials during the production process. 25 Because of the integrated nature of continuous 166 manufacturing processes, the quality unit can make a scientific determination that two or more 167 unit operations can be considered a single significant phase of manufacturing. This decision 168 should be made before initiating manufacturing, and it should be based on process 169 understanding. For example, in batch manufacturing of a solid oral drug product, blend 170 uniformity should typically be assessed before in-process materials continue to the compression 171 step. However, in continuous manufacturing, a manufacturer could conduct sampling and testing 172 at an appropriate point in the process (e.g., at the tablet press feed frame or after compression) to 173 evaluate the adequacy of mixing to ensure batch uniformity and homogeneity. Then, the quality 174 unit can determine whether to approve or reject the in-process material either before or after the 175 compression stage. Manufacturers should have robust understanding of the process, including 176 system dynamics. This will help manufacturers ensure that the sampling frequency is sufficiently 177
candidates.context: Continuous manufacturing and batch manufacturing could have different control strategies to 153 ensure batch uniformity and drug product integrity. Both continuous manufacturing and batch 154 manufacturing generally involve multiple manufacturing steps that physically or chemically 155 transform in-process materials. Typically, with a batch manufacturing process, in-process 156 materials can be easily isolated between each manufacturing step. This allows greater access for 157 sampling and testing of in-process materials before or after each step. However, given the 158 process design for continuous manufacturing, isolating in-process materials may not be feasible. 159 representative to draw a statistically valid conclusion about the quality of the in-process 178 materials and the drug product. 179

As part of FDA’s mission to protect and promote the public health, FDA is committed to 229 supporting and enabling pharmaceutical innovation and modernization. As the science 230 supporting innovative in-process control tools and methods continues to develop, FDA 231 anticipates that these scientific advancements can be leveraged to pursue in-process control 232 strategies that increasingly rely on process models. Based on the challenges associated with these 233 approaches, FDA encourages industry representatives and manufacturers to contact FDA if they 234 are interested in using alternative control strategies.
